title: Streaks and Clumps
objective: After this level you can explain why truly random sequences contain more streaks and clusters than people expect.
summary: Randomness is streaky: 200 real tosses typically hold a run of about eight, while fakes rarely pass five. Basketball's hot hand, once called an illusion, is still debated.

cards.headline: A teacher can spot fake coin tosses just by their streaks.
cards.body: Half a class tosses a real coin 200 times. The other half makes up 200 tosses. With one simple check, the teacher sorts most of them correctly. The giveaway? The fakes are too tidy.

cards.headline: Real randomness is streaky
cards.body: In 200 real tosses, the longest run of all heads or all tails is typically about eight. Students inventing tosses rarely write a run longer than five, because long runs don't feel random. Statistician Mark Schilling ran this test in his classes and sorted real from fake about 85% of the time. Real chance clumps; people smooth it out.

cards.headline: Why streaks turn up anyway
cards.body: Level 23 showed that any one long run is rare before it starts. But 200 flips give a run many places to start, so somewhere a run of several heads in a row is almost bound to appear. A streak on its own isn't a sign that something is off. It's what randomness looks like.

cards.fact: Is the hot hand real? Still argued.
cards.context: Basketball fans believe a player who has just made shots is more likely to make the next. A famous 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called that an illusion. In 2018, economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the study had counted streaks in a subtly biased way; correcting it reversed the conclusion. Whether fans overrate the hot hand is still open.

cards.headline: Streaks: expected
learned: Fakes rarely pass five in a row
The hot hand is still debated

questions.prompt: Match each with what the coin-toss test found.

pairs.right: Rarely write a run longer than five

questions.explanation: In 200 real tosses the longest run is typically about eight. Students inventing tosses rarely write a run longer than five, and Mark Schilling sorted real from fake about 85% of the time.

questions.prompt: How does a long streak end up in 200 random flips, even though any one streak is rare?

options.label: Coins build up momentum after a few heads
options.rationale: Flips are independent: a coin builds up nothing.

options.label: With so many places a run could start, one almost always does
Random flips alternate, then suddenly repeat
options.rationale: Random flips follow no pattern of alternating.

options.label: Streaks only happen with unfair coins
options.rationale: Fair coins produce streaks too; that is what randomness looks like.

questions.explanation: Each run is rare in advance, but 200 flips give a run many chances to start, so a run of several is almost bound to appear.

questions.prompt: Why is a basketball player's streak harder to judge than a fair coin's streak (Level 25)?

options.label: Players never have streaks
options.rationale: Players do have streaks; the question is whether they mean anything.

options.label: Coins are streakier than players
options.rationale: The comparison is about whether chances change, not how streaky.

options.label: A coin's flips are independent; a player's chances might really change
Basketball points come in 2s and 3s
options.rationale: Scoring has nothing to do with whether streaks are real.

questions.explanation: A coin keeps no score, so its streaks mean nothing. For a player, the hot hand says a hit could raise the chance of the next hit, and that is still argued.
